validated_work_order.approach:
Two files. One declaration in the stylesheet, and one abstraction in the test file that every stylesheet pin in it then uses, so that at the end of this change there is no second CSS parser left in the suite. Plus the repair that makes the suite green so any of it can be verified. The diagnosis is settled and this round does not reopen it.

R1 — ONE RULE ABOUT THE TERMINATING SEMICOLON, STATED ONCE. `declarations(body, prop)` treats a trailing chunk after the last `;` as a declaration, and every pin that reads through it therefore stays GREEN when a declaration loses its terminator. It is a STATED LOOSENING, and it is stated in exactly one place (AC-5) and quoted nowhere else except where a mutation is derived from it. Three things follow and all three say the same thing: matrix mutation 8 (the `;` off `.page-title`'s `line-height: 1.25`) is GREEN, mutation 9 (the `;` off `#main > *`'s `min-width: 0`) is GREEN, and contract case 5 is GREEN. What guards `#main > *`'s terminator afterwards is nothing, and out_of_scope says so in those words with the CSS rule that makes it correct — a pin that reddens on a missing terminator is a pin on punctuation rather than on the property it exists to protect, which is the defect class this ticket was filed about.

R2 — `.page-title` READS THROUGH `declarations()` TOO, so there is one reader rather than two behaviours. Today it is `const rule = /\.page-title\s*\{([^}]*)\}/.exec(css)` plus three `assert.match(rule[1], /prop:\s*value\s*;/)` calls — first-match only, terminator-required. After this change it collects EVERY non-nested rule whose comma-split selector part is exactly `.page-title` and asserts `declarations(rule.body, 'margin')` deepEqual `['0']`, `'font-size'` deepEqual `['1.4rem']`, `'line-height'` deepEqual `['1.25']` on each. This is what makes mutation 8 GREEN under R1, and it is also a strict improvement: appending `.page-title { margin: 4rem; }` to the end of the stylesheet is green under first-match and breaks the page. That is matrix mutation 13. The conversion preserves the assertion's meaning, so it is not an exception to AC-6, which constrains meaning and not spelling; AC-6 names it anyway so no reviewer has to infer it.

R3 — THE SIX EXISTING PINS KEEP NESTED RULES IN THEIR MIGRATED COLLECTIONS. This is the correction that matters most and the one the proposal did not make. Today all six collect their rules with `[...css.matchAll(/<selector>\s*\{([^}]*)\}/g)]`, which matches a rule wherever it sits, including inside an `@media` block. I verified the coverage is live rather than theoretical: appending `@media (max-width: 900px) { .table-scroll { overflow-x: visible; } }` to src/web/styles.css reads 70 pass / 2 fail, the extra failure being test 66. AC-9 collects NON-NESTED rules, because the media-nested `.awaiting-list li` rule must not be dragged into a value assertion. An implementer who applies that filter to the six as well — the natural reading of 'one reader, one rule' — silently deletes six live nested-override checks, and the suite goes green on exactly the defect this ticket exists to close. So: the six keep EVERY rule, top-level or nested, that matches their selector; the non-nested filter belongs to the new `.awaiting-list` pin alone and is for the reason AC-9 gives. Matrix mutation 14 pins it.

R4 — THE REPAIR FOR THE PRE-EXISTING RED USES THE FILE'S OWN IDIOM. Replace `/<li class="approval-card">/` with the token test the card pin already uses 15 lines below it: extract the class attribute, split it on whitespace, assert the resulting Set contains `approval-card`, and separately assert the element carries `data-testid="approval-card"` per .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md. The proposed regex `/<li\b[^>]*\bclass="[^"]*\bapproval-card\b[^"]*"/` is NOT used: I ran it against `/<li class="approval-card">/` on five inputs and it accepts `<li class="approval-card-extra">` and `<li class="not-approval-card">` while the old form rejects both, because `\b` after `approval-card` matches at a hyphen boundary. That is a new false negative on the rename axis #71 finding 2 was filed about, and the token form is immune to it while still matching the shipped markup.

A. Add `overflow-wrap: anywhere;` to the EXISTING `.awaiting-list li` rule in src/web/styles.css, in place among its display / gap / border / border-radius / padding declarations. Do NOT add a second rule with the same selector: the new pin collects every non-nested rule on that selector that declares the property and asserts the value on each, so a second rule reads as RED against the value assertion (matrix mutation 3) — that is the mechanism, and it is NOT the conflict check, which exempts the whole collected set by design.

B. Add four shared helpers near the top of test/web/pages.test.js, beside H1_HOOK (line 23) and mainOf (line 37), and route all eight stylesheet read sites through them. Only the plumbing moves, with the changes named in AC-6 named explicitly.

  `readStylesheet()` — the single readFileSync of src/web/styles.css, returning the SOURCE STRING. Every one of the eight sites becomes `const css = readStylesheet();`, the shape they have today, and the parse is one call on top. It returns the string rather than the parsed rules on purpose: the `length > 0` guards and failure messages at lines 1656, 1664, 1702, 1760, 1767, 1804 and 1821 are about the file, and AC-8's grep then means exactly what it says. Line 1611's readFileSync is NOT migrated: it reads test/web/pages.test.js itself inside the H1_HOOK call-site pin, which is why the `readFileSync` count is 10 and the stylesheet count is 8.

  `cssRules(source)` — strip /* */ with the SAME expression the card pin uses today at line 1696 (`css.replace(/\/\*[\s\S]*?\*\//g, ' ')`), then walk with a brace stack. A frame whose selector starts with '@' is a BLOCK whose children are rules; any other frame is a rule whose body is declarations. ';' terminates a declaration inside a rule and a prelude inside an at-rule. Nested rules are emitted with their own selector and a nested flag meaning 'not at top level'. At-rule frames are not emitted. Every rule carries a source index. ONE EXCEPTION, and it is in the shipped file today: a block whose prelude is `@keyframes` (or `@-webkit-keyframes`) contains KEYFRAME STEPS, not style rules — skip its children entirely rather than emitting `0%` / `100%` as rules, which the generic branch would otherwise do. A `0%` selector matches nothing on a comma-split `===` comparison, so the mis-emission is harmless to every pin today, but it puts junk into the one structure every other helper depends on and the shipped file has a keyframes block at styles.css:336-340, so the spec is wrong as written and cheap to make right. TWO OTHER FAILURE MODES PRODUCE PLAUSIBLE OUTPUT AND NEITHER SHOWS UP UNTIL A PIN DEPENDS ON IT: accumulating the prelude through a rule body concatenates `width: 100vw;` onto the selector of the next nested rule, and a reader that appends nested text to the parent body instead of descending into it drops every nested rule and reinstates the at-rule blind spot exactly — matrix mutations 3 and 4 are both green under that second bug while passing every test in the file as written today. This order pins NO magic rule count: a total breaks on every future stylesheet edit for no semantic reason and would not have caught either, because a reader that mangles nested selectors can still return the right number and one that drops nested rules can still return a different right number.

  `declarations(body, prop)` — one property's values from an already comment-stripped body, anchored on a declaration boundary (start of body, or after a ';') rather than a bare substring, with a trailing chunk after the last ';' treated as a declaration. THE REASONS FOR THE ANCHORING ARE MEASURED, and one commonly cited reason is false: 'min-width' is NOT a substring of 'min-height'. The reasons that are real, both green today: (a) a rule with no min-width at all but a comment naming one reads as ['16ch'], count 1, GREEN — the BUG-1 state passing the BUG-1 pin, because the min-width pin does not strip comments while the card pin beside it does; (b) a comment standing beside a real declaration is consumed as the declaration, so widths comes back ['0','16ch'] where the real floor is 16ch. The third thing the boundary buys is the custom-property case: a bare substring search matches `--min-width: 16ch` and a boundary-anchored one does not, in a stylesheet whose `:root` declares seventeen custom properties. The trailing-chunk clause is R1 and nothing else.

  `conflictingOverrides(rules, pinned, selectors, prop)` — the card pin's override loop at lines 1717-1720, lifted out of that test's body and corrected. The property is a fourth argument and the filter `declarations(other.body, prop).length > 0` runs INSIDE, because the card pin's existing `/overflow-wrap\s*:/` filter at line 1699 is what makes the comment above it true — a rule that cannot override the card classes does not turn the suite red. Take the property away and you get one of two failures: drop the filter and a narrow-viewport padding tweak on a pinned selector turns the suite red for a declaration that cannot change the property, re-breaking a tolerance #71 added on purpose; or hardcode overflow-wrap inside and the non-wrap pins get a check that can never fire. `pinned` is the rule or the SET of rules the calling pin has already asserted on, and every member is exempt — without the exemption the fix itself would be reported as an override of itself. A conflict is reported for any rule other than the pinned set, at ANY source index, top-level or nested, declaring `prop` on a comma-split selector part equal to a member of `selectors`. Symmetric in source order, because an override authored above the pinned rule wins at narrow viewports exactly as one below does, and the shipped forced-colors carve-out is the one existing case of that shape. The nested half is the fix for review finding 3 and is matrix mutations 4 and 11.

  THE SELECTOR LOOKUP MUST ANCHOR ON THE SELECTOR'S END — compare a comma-split part to the pinned selector with `===`, never `selector.includes(pinnedSelector)`. '.opportunity-roww' and '.tenant-names' both contain their pinned selector as a substring; the current `\s*\{` anchors give the pins their rename protection today, and a substring lookup deletes it across all eight pins at once, invisibly.

  WHERE THE CONFLICT CHECK IS CALLED, and this is the design decision that matters most. Call it at the card pin (1691) and at the new `.awaiting-list` pin ONLY. Lines 1652 (`#main > *`), 1663 (`.table-scroll`), 1756 (`.approval-actions`), 1766 (`.approval-actions input`), 1801 (`.journal-drawer-body`) and 1818 (`.tenant-name`) each already collect EVERY rule matching their selector — top-level and nested, per R3 — and assert the property on every one of them, so their every-match loop IS their selector's override check, and it is stronger than a same-selector conflict check because it also catches a rule declaring the WRONG value. Because the helper exempts the pinned set, and on those six the pinned set is every rule that could ever match, a call there could never fire: dead code that reads as coverage. Put one line in each of those six tests' comments saying the every-match loop is that selector's override check, so the absence reads as a decision. The distinction the comment depends on is pinned by contract case 7 so it cannot rot silently.

  THE CARD PIN KEEPS ITS OWN PRE-FILTER — the one place a migration could false-red on a correct stylesheet. Today the card pin builds its candidate set, filters it with `/overflow-wrap\s*:/.test(rule.body)`, and only then calls `.find()`. That filter is load-bearing: without it `find()` returns `.approval-card, .experiment-card` at styles.css:375-383 — the border / padding / display rule, two classes, no `overflow-wrap` at all — and both the selector-set equality assertion against CARD_CLASSES and the `deepEqual(values, ['anywhere'])` assertion go RED on the shipped file. This pre-filter is DISTINCT from the one inside `conflictingOverrides`, and both survive the migration. It is named in AC-6 so nobody simplifies it away.

  THE FORCED-COLORS PIN, the third place that needs care, and the loosening is accepted on purpose and pinned. The current regex at pages.test.js:360 is `/@media\s*\(forced-colors:\s*active\)\s*\{[^@]*?#main:focus\s*\{([^}]*)\}/`, and its `[^@]*?` means it only finds the carve-out when it is the first thing in the block. The reader finds it wherever it sits, so the rewrite is strictly MORE PERMISSIVE. The assertions that carry the meaning are unchanged — the carve-out exists, declares `outline: 2px solid CanvasText`, and comes after the bare #main:focus rule at equal specificity, both selectors being 1,1,0 — and a mutation that puts another nested rule before the carve-out must still pass, so the loosening is a stated behaviour. The test's comment says the parser's strictness changed, not the assertion. Keep the `length > 0` guard on the not-at-top-level lookup specifically, so a reader regression that stopped descending into at-rules cannot make this test pass vacuously on a file with no carve-out at all. The source-order assertion at pages.test.js:372-377 is the only thing in the suite that pins WHY the carve-out wins, and its comment says so; it must survive the rewrite as a comparison of the two rules' SOURCE INDICES rather than of character offsets, deliberately, not by accident. `grep -n '#main:focus' src/web/styles.css` returns 117 (a comment mention with no brace after it, which the current `search(/#main:focus\s*\{/)` skips), 131 (top level) and 136 (the first rule inside the `@media (forced-colors: active)` opened at 135), so 'exactly one top-level and exactly one not at top level' is a count the shipped file satisfies today.

  THE NEW `.awaiting-list` PIN, in the house style of `#main > *` and `.tenant-name` rather than a whole-body assertion, and in ONE test. In order: (a) collect every rule that is NOT nested, whose comma-split selector part is `.awaiting-list` or `.awaiting-list li`, and whose body declares overflow-wrap — the property filter is part of the COLLECTION predicate, not only inside the helper, and the test's comment must say that in those terms, because the media-nested rule's selector part IS exactly '.awaiting-list li' and an unfiltered collection takes it in, at which point `deepEqual(['anywhere'])` fails and the suite goes red for a padding declaration; (b) require the collection NON-EMPTY, with a message that says so, so deleting the declaration and leaving a comment is red — matrix mutation 1, and today's `.awaiting-list li` rule has zero overflow-wrap declarations in it, so (b) is what turns the current state red rather than vacuous; (c) require each collected rule's overflow-wrap values to deepEqual `['anywhere']`; (d) run `conflictingOverrides(rules, collected, ['.awaiting-list', '.awaiting-list li', '.awaiting-list li strong', '.awaiting-list li span'], 'overflow-wrap')` and require it to report nothing. Two strictnesses with their costs recorded in out_of_scope: `.awaiting-list` (the ul) is in the collection's selector set, because `overflow-wrap` is inherited and the pin must not report a correct fix on the parent as absent — that is matrix mutation 7 and it is GREEN on purpose; and the collection requires the declaration at TOP LEVEL, because a fix authored only inside `@media (max-width: 900px)` satisfies the new pin in full AND satisfies the whole browser sweep at 320 / 375 / 414, all of which are inside that query, while the defect is not inherently narrow-viewport — that is matrix mutation 5 and it is RED on purpose.

  (e) the render half, in the same test, AS A LINK ASSERTION AND NOTHING MORE. Use `seededRepos(prefix)`, which creates tenant_demo and the seeded decisions, NOT bare `freshRepos()`, which has no tenant: on a seeded fixture `repos.tenants.list()` reads exactly `['tenant_demo']` with three decisions of which exactly one (`dec_seed_awaiting_1`) is unevaluated, and `decisionsOf` at src/web/pages.js:614-619 is `if (!tenant) { return []; }`, so a fixture without a tenant renders the empty branch with no `class="awaiting-list"` anywhere. Before rendering, assert that `repos.tenants.list()` is exactly one row and its id is `tenant_demo`, with a message saying the fixture's tenant selection is load-bearing for `firstTenant()` — that assertion stops a future seed adding a second tenant from repointing the whole page, and it is the same check that proves a seeded database was served. Then create ONE further decision on top of the seed through the EIGHT-FIELD `repos.decisions.create(...)`, whose decision_id is `'dec_' + 'q'.repeat(136)` (140 unbreakable characters), and assert that /journal at override 'partial' emits `class="awaiting-list"` with at least one `<li data-decision-id` and that the long id appears inside the awaiting `<ul>` segment. Count assertions are NON-EQUALITY throughout: the id also reaches the journal table row and the Open button, so the page carries `data-decision-id` seven times on a clean boot and a second decision changes that number. The claim is 'the list renders and the id is in it', not a count.

  (f) the thirteen-mutation list ALSO LIVES IN THE FILE, as a comment block above the new pin. A matrix that exists only in a plan document is deleted with the plan and enforces nothing; the one durable home available to this change is the test it pins.

The direction of an UNDER-matching reader failure is safe — a parser that stops matching makes the `length > 0` guards fire, so the suite goes red rather than green — but that is not the whole risk: a reader that over-emits (the keyframes case) or that returns the wrong rule from a lookup (the card pin's dropped pre-filter) does not trip any guard at all. The blast radius is a 1904-line test file. This is why tests[]'s FIRST instruction is the matrix.

The six existing pins losing their nested-override coverage is the single most likely way this change makes the suite weaker while claiming to make it stronger. It is specified in approach R3, named in AC-6(ii) and pinned by matrix mutation 14, but it is a change of habit — the new pin filters on `nested` and the six must not — and it is exactly the kind of thing that is right in review and wrong in a hurry.

The ch-only narrowing will redden someone's legitimate edit one day, and the person who hits it will be under time pressure. It is declared in AC-6, in files[](1), in the AC-5 matrix, in risks and in out_of_scope rather than in one place, precisely so that finding it costs a grep and not an argument. The issue's own review proposed a unit conversion instead and named 160px as a value it would accept; this order rejects the conversion, because 1ch = 10.18px is a property of the resolved system-ui font and differs on macOS and Windows, and pays for the rejection in redness. A maintainer may reasonably reverse that.

The forced-colors rewrite is strictly MORE PERMISSIVE. The current regex's `[^@]*?` only finds the carve-out when it is the first thing in the block, and the reader finds it wherever it sits. The assertions that carry the meaning are unchanged, so it is a stated behaviour rather than a fix, and the test's comment says the parser's strictness changed and not the assertion.

The new pin's collection is stricter than the page strictly needs in one direction and looser in another, and both are declared. Stricter: it requires the declaration at top level, so a correct narrow-viewport-only fix reads red. Looser: it accepts the fix on the parent `.awaiting-list`, so it cannot distinguish an inherited fix from one authored on the wrong element. Neither is an oversight and both are in out_of_scope.

out_of_scope: The `#main > *` pin's terminating semicolon is guarded by NOTHING after this change, and that is the intended answer rather than an open gap. AC-5's rule lets a declaration whose terminating `;` is missing still be a declaration, so matrix mutation 9 is GREEN and no assertion anywhere requires the terminator. The reason is that a declaration's terminating semicolon is OPTIONAL when it is the last one in a block — `.page-title { margin: 0; line-height: 1.25 }` and the same rule with the semicolon parse to an identical declaration list in every browser — so a pin that reddens on the difference is a pin on punctuation rather than on the property it exists to protect, and requiring it would make a legal stylesheet edit fail CI. The `min-width: 0` value itself is still asserted, on every rule whose selector part is exactly `#main > *`, which is the property the pin is for. A reviewer who wants the terminator required can add a strict variant of `declarations()` and call it from the `#main > *` and `.table-scroll` pins, and should then also expect to name `.page-title` as a second departure from AC-6 — that is the option the last review set out, and this order rejects it on the CSS grounds above rather than on cost.

It DOES have a `@keyframes` block at styles.css:336-340, which is why contract case 10 exists — an earlier version of this order asserted the shipped file was free of at-rule shapes the reader had not seen, and that was true of the four it named and silent on the one that was there.

Whether the headless figures match a headed browser, and which scrollbar configuration a QA browser will present. Two prior agents measured different clientWidth values for the same page on the same runner. The layout mechanism is not browser-specific and the defect and the fix are confirmed from the CSS, but AC-2 and AC-10 are written as invariants by selector for exactly this reason and name no pixel.

Whether a decision_id in a real deployment reaches 120+ unbreakable characters. The repository accepts any string and the API resolves a tenant from free-text request headers, so a long id is constructible and was constructed in the recorded QA run; whether it occurs in practice is a production question. The defect is real and reachable either way and its severity does not depend on how often it fires.

Whether `.journal-calibration` overflows. The order's expectation is that it does not, because the precision and false-intervention strings are formatted from counts and ratios rather than stored free text, and that expectation is a reading of the formatter and not a measurement. This is the one finding of the ticket's seven that is deferred rather than closed, and the uncertainty is inherited rather than introduced.

Whether anything outside this repository reads the `approval.requested` raw event the pendingApprovalRepos fixture appends. Within src/, test/ and scripts/ nothing does. If an external consumer exists, removing the append from a test fixture is still correct, but it cannot be seen from inside the tree. residual_risks: QA should read this first, and then this one. The layout defect has NO automated coverage of any kind. The new pin is a declaration pin; the render half reads no stylesheet and passes with or without the declaration; the repository has no browser driver. Everything else in this order's automated half is about the PARSER, not about the page. That is stated plainly because it is the single largest thing this order cannot close, and softening it into partial coverage is the same error an earlier round's review caught.

THE HOLE, CHOSEN RATHER THAN MISSED, IN ITS GENERAL FORM. The new pin is anchored on the li's own selector, so ANY rule elsewhere declaring overflow-wrap on a selector matching a DESCENDANT of the li reinstates the page overflow with a green suite. `.panel strong { overflow-wrap: normal; }` is the in-house-plausible form and qa_script step 5 demonstrates it on purpose. The more likely form of the same mistake, and the one the order does not name anywhere, is `white-space: nowrap` on the panel: it defeats inheritance outright and the pin is silent on it, because a property filter on `overflow-wrap` cannot see a different property. There is also no finite watch list that closes this, and if a future edit changes the awaiting ul from `display: grid` to `display: flex`, the min-content mechanism the whole fix rests on disappears while the pin stays green. These are the first three things QA should go looking for after step 5.

The migration is unexecuted, and the reader is a single point of failure for every stylesheet assertion in a 1904-line test file. The under-matching direction is safe — a parser that stops matching makes the `length > 0` guards fire — but the blast radius is the file, over-matching does not trip any guard, and the contract test covers fixture strings rather than the shipped stylesheet. This is the risk most likely to be skimmed and the reason tests[] puts the matrix first. AC-5 is not machine-observed and the work-order schema has no value that says so; the disclaimer lives in the criterion's own text and in the test-file comment block the order requires.

Every browser figure in this order was measured in headless Chromium over raw CDP, by the reporter and by prior rounds, because the repository has no browser driver and its only runtime dependency is express. Font rasterization and scrollbar metrics differ from a headed browser, and two prior agents measured different clientWidth values for the same runner. QA should confirm the invariant rather than take the figures. The three widths (320, 375, 414) are the reporter's, not a boundary this order chose: docs/ui.md places the journal's narrow layout at under 900px, so a future media query tightening padding below 320px reinstates the defect with no criterion reaching it.

The four helpers carry the whole automated half of this ticket. AC-7 pins their contract on fixture strings, but a fixture test only pins the cases someone thought of: a comma inside a functional pseudo-class, an at-rule nested inside an at-rule, a semicolon inside quotes or a url(), and @supports are unhandled by anything here.

The ch-only narrowing will redden someone's legitimate edit one day, and the person who hits it will be under time pressure. It is declared in five places rather than one precisely so that finding costs a grep and not an argument.

The narrow-viewport sweep runs headless with no forced-colors emulation. A forced-colors check was judged unnecessary — forced-colors forces colour and contrast and does not alter overflow-wrap or intrinsic sizing — but that is reasoning, not a measurement, and the stylesheet does carry a forced-colors carve-out for #main:focus, which this change rewrites the test for.

A QA agent who re-runs the boot step against an already-seeded /tmp/qa77.db, or who posts a second long decision, will see different counts from the ones recorded here. Every figure in qa_script is an observation on a clean boot, and the criteria are written as non-zero rather than as equal-to-a-number precisely so that a second run is not a false failure. The one number that was load-bearing — the 225280-byte seed size — and the test total in AC-3 are both gone for the same reason.
validated_work_order.debate_summary:
The critique returned 'flawed' with ten findings, three of them blocking. I re-ran the load-bearing ones myself rather than accepting them, upheld eight (one of them in a narrower form than it was filed), partly upheld one, and dismissed one as unexpressible. I found four defects the critique did not name. The design survives; what changed is four stated mechanisms, a regression the migration does not answer, and a repair that was described as a strengthening and is a relaxation. This is not a tidy consensus and I am not presenting it as one — the plan and the critique still disagree about the shape of the ticket, and that disagreement is live.

WHAT THE CRITIQUE GOT RIGHT, AND THE BIGGEST THING IN IT IS THE ONE THAT WILL COST THE MOST IF IT SHIPS. Its finding that the six existing pins would silently lose nested-override coverage is CORRECT and I verified it rather than reasoning about it: appending `@media (max-width: 900px) { .table-scroll { overflow-x: visible; } }` to src/web/styles.css reads 70 pass / 2 fail with test 66 the extra failure, so the coverage is live today. The plan justifies not calling `conflictingOverrides` at those six on the grounds that 'their every-match loop IS the same coverage' — which is true ONLY if the migrated collections keep nested rules, and the plan never says whether they do, while AC-9 filters on `nested` for the new pin. An implementer who applies one filter everywhere, which is the natural reading of 'one reader, one rule', retires six live checks. The order now states the requirement in three places (approach R3, AC-6's named change (ii), and a new matrix row 14) and the implementer has one command that settles it. I did not accept the critique's preferred fix, which was to add the conflict check to all six; that check could never fire there, because the helper exempts the pinned set and on those six the pinned set is every rule that could ever match. I kept the plan's design and fixed its silence, which is a smaller change than the critique asked for and, I think, the right one — the every-match loop is a STRONGER override check than a same-selector conflict check, because it also catches a rule declaring the wrong value.

Its second blocking finding, that mutation 3's stated mechanism is impossible, is CORRECT and I want to be plain that this is the fourth time this order has shipped a mechanism a reviewer has to disprove, and the last review was returned for exactly that. The collection IS the pinned set, so a rule that joined it is exempt from `conflictingOverrides` by the plan's own contract 7; the value assertion is what fires. The verdict RED was right and the mechanism was not, and the same false justification appeared in files[](1). Both are corrected. I am recording the pattern rather than the individual fixes because a plan that keeps shipping untrue mechanisms is telling the reader something about the rest of its specifications too — which is part of why this confidence is 76 and not the 80 the proposal asked for.

Its third blocking finding, that `cssRules()` has no case for `@keyframes` and the shipped stylesheet has one at styles.css:336, is CORRECT and I verified it. But I DISAGREE WITH ITS SEVERITY, and this is the one substantive downgrade I made. The critique calls it blocking and 'a latent wrong-output case'. Emitting `0%` and `100%` as rules affects nothing today: no pin matches a bare-percentage selector on a comma-split `===` comparison, no source-index pair the order depends on is disturbed, and no matrix verdict changes. It is a real gap in a spec for a single point of failure, and the fix is one clause in the reader plus one contract case, so it is in. I am recording that I graded it major rather than blocking, because a finding that cannot change any verdict in the matrix cannot be the thing that rejects the plan, and because the proposal's `unknowns` sentence it attacks — 'the shipped file has none of the four' — is actually TRUE of the four it names. The sentence is silent about @keyframes, not false about what it says.

WHERE THE CRITIQUE WAS RIGHT AND ITS FIX WAS NOT EXPRESSIBLE. Its finding that AC-5's `verify: test` label reads as a claim the suite gates the matrix is right in substance and unfixable as proposed: it asked for a `human` value in the work-order enum, and the enum is browser | test | api with anything outside it dropped, which I can see in the same limits the plan quotes. The plan already answers the substance — AC-5 says in its own text that the matrix is a person-run procedure that `npm run sdlc:verify` cannot observe and that the schema has no value meaning 'a human reads this'. What I DID take from that finding is its sharper second point, which the plan had not answered: a matrix that exists only in a plan document is deleted with the plan and enforces nothing. The fourteen rows now also live as a comment block in the new test, which is in files[] and survives the merge. That is the one durable home available inside this change, and I am aware it is a comment, not an executable check.

WHERE I PARTLY UPHELD IT. Its finding that the repair for the pre-existing red test 68 is weaker than the assertion it replaces, despite files[](2) calling it 'strictly stronger… not a relaxation', is CORRECT and I ran both matchers to confirm rather than reading the regex: `\b` after `approval-card` matches at a hyphen boundary, so the new form accepts `approval-card-extra` and `not-approval-card` where the old one rejects both. The repair is now the file's own idiom — extract the class attribute, split on whitespace, assert the token Set — and the false sentence is gone. Its finding that AC-2 lists five surfaces when only `/journal?state=partial` can be moved by this change is CORRECT; I have added `/journal`, which does render the long id, and the criterion now says plainly which surface is acceptance and which five are no-regression guards against #48 and #67. Its two minor findings — the uncounted ninth readFileSync at line 1611, and AC-3's exact test total — I took both, and the second I took as a consistency point against the plan itself: the plan dropped the exact seed byte count for exactly the reason AC-3's total should go, and holding its own criterion to a looser standard than its QA step is the kind of thing that makes the rest of the numbers harder to trust.

WHERE I DISAGREE WITH THE CRITIQUE, and it is the same disagreement the last two rounds recorded and it is not resolved. The critique's third major finding, that the issue's review calls the helper extraction 'Optional, and not worth blocking on' and the plan never engages it, is factually right about the issue text and I have answered it on the record in alternatives_considered. It is not a reason to shrink the work, and the reason is not defensiveness: the review that wrote that sentence took its own advice for each of the four findings it filed, so 'optional' was about the EXTRACTION as the vehicle for findings that were not optional. Against that, the new pin needs a stylesheet parse, and a fresh local parser inside one test adds a fifth parser to a file with four hand-rolled ones — a net increase in the class this ticket exists to close. The product fix is one declaration that ships either way. I considered `scope_changed` to maintainer and rejected it, because a split puts one line of CSS in a different ticket from the parser that pins it, which is how the false 'measured and safe' entry that started this chain got written. The migration is unexecuted and its blast radius is a 1904-line file, and I am not going to answer a real risk by making the plan smaller — the honest response is the matrix as the first instruction, the comment block, and a confidence number that says what I do not know.

WHAT I FOUND THAT NEITHER DOCUMENT DID. The card pin's `find()` depends on a pre-filter the migration puts at risk: filter the candidate set on `/overflow-wrap\s*:/` and the lookup returns the four-class rule; drop the filter and it returns `.approval-card, .experiment-card` at styles.css:375-383, two classes and no `overflow-wrap`, and both the selector-set and the value assertion false-red on a correct stylesheet. It is a false positive, the cheaper failure, but it is introduced for free by a migration presented as meaning-preserving, and the plan never mentions it. It is now named in approach B and in AC-6(iii) so nobody simplifies it away. Second, the fix's own mechanism is unstated: `.awaiting-list li` is itself `display: grid`, so the `<strong>` carrying the decision_id is a grandchild grid item with its own automatic minimum, and the declaration works by INHERITANCE into it — the same structure the four-card rule at 394-399 already relies on for `.approval-card` at 375-383. `min-width: 0`, the other standard fix, is not mentioned anywhere in the order and was never rejected in writing. files[](1) now says all of it, so the next reader knows the fix reaches a grandchild through a nested grid on purpose and not by accident.
